parts.note: a trench is a long narrow ditch
a worker is one caste of ant, so 'maybe' flags the example

explanation.surface: Someone who digs ditches for a living turns out to have a sharp mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ditch worker' reads as one job title, but the two words are separate pieces; 'being' simply links them to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a trenchant remark is sharp and cutting, just as an incisive one is.

clue.text: Plant built with odd omissions in the end

indicators.note: the picked letters are placed inside the word for the end

parts.note: the tip of something is its very end

indicators.note: leaving out the odd-numbered letters keeps only the second and fourth

explanation.surface: A factory was put up, though strange things were left out when it was finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' wants to be a factory beside 'built'; it is the flower. 'with odd omissions' keeps the even letters of 'built', and 'in' drops them into a word for the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: it is a spring-flowering bulb, one member of the vegetable kingdom.

clue.text: Admit academic robe's no good at university

indicators.note: no good means the letter standing for good is absent from the robe

parts.note: a gown is the robe worn by academics
in British usage a student who is up is in residence at university

explanation.surface: Concede that the scholar's gown is useless on campus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no' removes G from GOWN. 'Up' is the British (chiefly Oxbridge) term for being in residence at university.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to confess to something is to acknowledge responsibility for it.

parts.note: a snooker player may put backspin on the cue ball, which is called screwing it; read as verb plus object the phrase gives the two halves

explanation.surface: A remark that an oddball is something a person at the baize might be.
explanation.walkthrough: The sentence is left unfinished on purpose: what a snooker player may do is apply backspin (screw) to the ball, and that verb and object together spell the eccentric.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang noun, originally American, for a zany or crazy person.

parts.note: something over is left as surplus, extra
money that is owed is due

explanation.surface: An additional sum that someone owes has still not turned up.
explanation.definitionFit: Paraphrase: a train or baby that is late has not come when expected.

definitions.meaning: a passenger riding in a railway coach is inside the locomotive-hauled vehicle
an idiom for in progress, already set in motion

explanation.definitionFit: Double sense: literally aboard a railway service, and idiomatically describing plans already in motion.

clue.text: Groomed by extraordinary carpenter in work

indicators.note: something extraordinary is out of the usual order, so the two words before it are rearranged

parts.note: Chips is the traditional nickname for a carpenter, especially a ship's carpenter

explanation.surface: A remarkable woodworker on the job has smartened someone up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extraordinary' rearranges GROOMED BY into GOODBYE MR. 'Work' is a literary work: James Hilton's 1934 novella about an English schoolmaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: it is a novel, hence a literary creation.

clue.text: Pipe to be attached to the two taps? Can't make a decision

indicators.note: the first piece is joined on to the front of the taps' names

parts.note: to pipe is to play a wind instrument, that is, to blow
a basin's two taps are labelled hot and cold

explanation.surface: A plumber dithers over fitting one pipe to both taps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be attached to' just joins the pieces. 'Pipe' looks like plumbing but is the verb for sounding a wind instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: someone who vacillates keeps switching between enthusiasm and reluctance.

clue.text: One may read this either way

indicators.note: the phrase reads the same forwards and backwards, so it can be read in either direction

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A text that can be interpreted in two ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'either way' says the letters are the same in both directions. It is a British term for a cosy novel of middle-class country life, named after the Aga cooker found in such kitchens.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: it is a genre of popular novel, something a person reads.

indicators.note: backed means the word for therefore is written backwards

parts.note: so means therefore
a weight that is supported is borne

explanation.surface: Someone duly gave a dramatist financial and moral support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' turns SO into OS. John Osborne wrote Look Back in Anger (1956), the play that launched Britain's 'angry young men'.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: John of that name was a leading British dramatist.

indicators.note: the word for movement comes after the word for fashion

parts.note: to fashion something is to make it
a shift is a movement from one position to another

explanation.surface: A short-lived political or artistic movement chasing the latest trend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fashion' is a verb here, to create, not a trend, and 'movement' is a simple change of position; 'following' only fixes their order.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a stopgap arrangement serves for the time being until something proper replaces it.

definitions.meaning: to combine separate things into a single whole
to join two people in wedlock

explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are synonyms: joining things into a single whole, and joining a couple in wedlock.

indicators.note: not left means the letter for left is taken away from the word for launch

parts.note: to launch a missile is to hurl it

explanation.surface: A motor boat is still out on the water, not abandoned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes L from HURL. 'Launch' looks like a boat but is the verb to throw.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: one of the five Great Lakes of North America.

clue.text: Get better soldiers in a time for reform

indicators.note: the two inner words sit between the article and the abbreviation for time

parts.note: to mend is to recover, get better
men is a common term for soldiers, the rank and file

explanation.surface: Troops need to recover within a set period so the army can be reorganised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reform' is a noun here, a change that improves, though the surface makes it a verb; 'in' is the container signal, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a noun: a change made to improve a law or document.

indicators.note: the letter for nothing goes inside the word for between

parts.note: to pass between two things is to go through them
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Say not a word in the interval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts O inside THROUGH. 'Utter' looks like a verb meaning speak but is the adjective meaning complete.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as an adjective: an out-and-out, complete rogue.

indicators.note: the letter I is thrown inside the name of the lough

parts.note: Lough Erne is a lake system in County Fermanagh, Northern Ireland; lough is the Irish word for lake

explanation.surface: I threw a lad into an Irish lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flung in' puts I inside ERNE, the lough in Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a male given name, short for Ernest.

clue.text: Trophy is broken by daughter bending shape of lip

parts.note: a cup is a sporting trophy

indicators.note: the letter for daughter splits the word 'is' in two

parts.note: D is the genealogical abbreviation for daughter
a bow is a bending of the body or a curve

explanation.surface: A girl smashes a sporting prize and it buckles into a mouth-like curve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken by' puts D inside IS. The term describes the double curve of the upper lip, like the love god's weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: Technical term for the double-curved outline of the upper mouth, named after an archer's weapon.

indicators.note: relaxed letters are loosened from their order and rearranged
not feminine means the letter for feminine is left out

parts.note: F is the grammatical abbreviation for feminine

explanation.surface: A stern face softens, though it is hardly womanly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes F from FEATURES, and 'relaxed' rearranges the remaining EATURES.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: stern and strict in manner or plain in style.

indicators.note: the word for row goes around the word for stray

parts.note: a tier is a row of seats
to err is to stray from the right path

explanation.surface: An argument breaks out over a lost mongrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' is a line of seats, not a quarrel, and 'stray' is the verb to wander, not a lost animal; 'about' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a type of small hound bred to dig out burrowing animals.

parts.note: to draw a cart is to tow it along
'this is it' means this is the crucial moment or thing

explanation.surface: That is to say, a tied match is what matters most.
explanation.walkthrough: 'draw' suggests a tied game but means pull.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a formal phrase meaning 'that is to say'.

indicators.note: mistreated letters are handled roughly and so rearranged

explanation.surface: Sadly, a pet store has been cruel to one of its animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mistreated' rearranges A SHOP ALAS. The breed is a small long-haired one from Tibet.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a small long-coated Tibetan breed.

clue.text: Fence built by friend at home, close to outbuilding

parts.note: a pal is a friend
someone who is in is at home

indicators.note: the close of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A mate puts up a barrier in his garden beside the shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'close to' takes the last letter of 'outbuilding'; 'built by' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a barrier made of upright pointed stakes.

indicators.note: done badly, the letters of the next two words come out in the wrong order

explanation.surface: A ship from Seoul sails with poor lights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly' rearranges LIT KOREAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a ship built to carry petroleum in bulk.

clue.text: Unwilling to change cloak before spring

indicators.note: the word for cloak is placed ahead of the word for spring

parts.note: to cloak something is to hide it
to spring is to bound, leap

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to swap their winter cape until the season turns.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue paints a garment and a season, but 'cloak' and 'spring' are both verbs: conceal and leap. 'before' only fixes their order.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: rigidly conventional and set in one's ways.

clue.text: Person supporting that woman through a depression

indicators.note: the pronoun passes through the middle of the other letters

parts.note: a dent is a hollow, a depression in a surface
her is the pronoun for that woman

explanation.surface: A friend stands by a woman during her spell of low spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'depression' is a physical hollow, not a low mood, and 'through' says the pronoun runs inside the rest rather than describing endurance.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a follower or backer of a cause or leader.

clue.text: Wilde hasn't succeeded in opening of act that is to be played

indicators.note: hasn't succeeded means the letter for succeeded is missing from the name

parts.note: Oscar is the first name of the playwright Wilde
S is the genealogical abbreviation for succeeded

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: The dramatist has failed with the first scene of a drama due to be staged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hasn't' removes S from OSCAR; 'opening of' gives the first letter of 'act'.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: it is a small egg-shaped wind instrument, something a musician performs on.

clue.text: A job extremely lucrative for James, say

parts.note: a post is a job, a position of employment

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: James, for one, has landed a very well-paid position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' takes the first and last letters of 'lucrative'. 'say' flags James as one example of the twelve.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: James was one of the twelve disciples sent out by Jesus.

clue.text: Friendliness shown by member in with one given the heave-ho

indicators.note: the word for member goes inside what remains of 'with'
to be given the heave-ho is to be thrown out, so the letter for one is ejected

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
an arm is a limb, a member of the body

explanation.surface: A club member is kind to a colleague who has just been sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given the heave-ho' is slang for being thrown out, here ejecting one letter from 'with'; 'in' then houses a limb, not a club member, in what is left (WTH).
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: cordiality and kindness of manner.

clue.text: Runs in a boy responsible for crime

indicators.note: the letter for runs goes inside the article plus the word for boy

parts.note: a son is a male child, a boy
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A lad who committed an offence is on the run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts R inside A SON; 'responsible for' only links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: deliberately setting fire to property is a criminal offence.

indicators.note: the article falls inside the word for hike

parts.note: a price hike is a rise
A is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Pick up an item while out on a country walk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'during' puts A inside RISE. 'hike' is an increase, not a walk.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to gather money together, as for a charity.
